newsitem.title: ROMANIA: France's Chirac backs Romania on West integration.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac backs Romania on West integration.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac on Saturday assured Romanians that Paris was fully behind their drive to secure quick acceptance into Western defence and economic institutions.

Chirac, the first Western leader to visit Romania in six years, has repeatedly promised to back the drive by President Emil Constantinescu and his centrist government to beat the odds and be among the first countries to join an expanded NATO.
"Tomorrow, your courageous efforts will bear fruit. Romania will enter the Atlantic alliance," Chirac told a polite audience of handpicked students at Bucharest University.
"It will be a full member of the European Union -- our great joint project for the 21st century. Europe will become for you a daily reality. France fully backs Romania's European aspirations."

Chirac has been cheered by Bucharest residents grown unused to the pomp of state visits under Constantinescu's ex-communist predecessor Ion Iliescu who was shunned by Western leaders during his seven years in office.

Chirac's every utterance has been laden with references to France's role in shaping the new Romanian state at the turn of the century and its cultural links with eastern Europe's only Latin nation. Romanian radio and television have saturated their programmes with French music and films during the two-day visit.
Iliescu, who took office after the execution of Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, told Chirac Romanians were united in seeking legitimacy by gaining entry to Western institutions.

"There will always be a consensus on foreign policy in Romania," he told the state-run Rompres news agency. "I assured the president that all political forces agreed on the necessity of integrating into European and Euro-Atlantic structures."
Even students who lived only a short period of their lives under Ceausescu made NATO and the EU central issues during an hour-long question-and-answer session with Chirac.

Chirac told a woman of 19 that enlarging NATO was part of rebuilding a Europe too long divided by communism. The first expansion wave to be decided in July, he said, should go beyond favoured candidates Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.
"France has adopted a strong position that the first wave should also take in Romania and perhaps Slovenia," he said.
Even Russia, he said, accepted the principle of expansion, but was insisting on a separate agreement with the Alliance to allay worries on how its interests might be affected.
"Russia is concerned about the means and applications of enlargement...and one can understand that," he said.
"(Russian President Boris) Yeltsin is open to enlargement on condition that a prior accord is signed with Russia."
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright acknowledged after talks this week in Moscow that no breakthrough had been achieved with the Kremlin over expansion.

Romania argues that its position on the Black Sea and proximity to Poland and ex-Soviet Ukraine make its inclusion a strategic trump card for NATO. It hopes Chirac can persuade Washington to reverse its reluctance to its rapid admission.

Romania appears to have improved its chances for early admission following Constantinescu's election, pledges to proceed with market reforms and the formal resolution of long-standing disputes with Hungary.
